title: How infalling gas reshapes planet-forming discs

sections.body: Protoplanetary discs are discs of gas and dust that surround young stars, and are the birthplaces of planets. In the classic picture of star and planet formation, protoplanetary discs form as an outcome of the conservation of angular momentum from an infalling envelope. It was thought that once this envelope completed infalling (within ~500kyr), the connection between the protostar and protoplanetary disc with the surrounding environment was severed. However, recent observations reveal that even relatively old systems (ages > 1Myr) are still actively accreting from the environment. How this infalling material impacts the structures and properties of protoplanetary discs is crucial for understanding the resulting impacts on the planet formation process, and whether infalling gas can also produce similar substructures as planets do.

sections.body:
What happens when infalling gas impacts the disc?

In Anatomy of a Fall (named after a French movie with the same name) my collaborators and I used three-dimensional smooth particle hydrodynamic (SPH) simulations to follow a narrow stream of gas, known as a streamer, as it collides with the disc. We found that the infalling streamer can indeed lead to some interesting phenomena. Below is a movie which shows an example of the simulations. You can see that when the streamer hits the disc, a lot of spiral arms are generated, and they rotate around the disc with different pattern speeds.

sections.alt: Simulation showing an infalling streamer of gas interacting the a protoplanetary disc. The interaction leads to the generation of spiral arms which move with various different pattern speeds.
sections.caption: Simulation showing an infalling streamer of gas interacting the a protoplanetary disc. The interaction leads to the generation of spiral arms which move with various different pattern speeds.

sections.body: We found that spiral arms launched by infall can look deceptively similar to those generated by multi-Jupiter mass planets. The figure below shows a comparison between the spiral arms seen in another one of my simulations compared with spiral arms launched by a multi-Jupiter mass planet from Dong et al. 2015. Although these spiral arms look very similar, there is a way we can tell them apart. Spiral arms launched by a planet should move with the same pattern speed as the planet itself. So if the planet takes 100 years to make a single orbit, so do the spiral arms. But we found that infall driven spirals do not have such simple pattern speeds: some spirals can be stationary on ~1000 year timescales, while other spiral arms move on much shorter timescales.

sections.alt: Side-by-side simulations showing a gas stream producing spiral arms in a disc on the left and a planet producing spiral arms on the right.
sections.caption: Two routes to similar-looking spiral arms. Left: the gas distribution in our infall simulation. Right: a simulated disc with spiral arms driven by a planet. Although they look similar, these spirals have different dynamical behaviors. Infall panel adapted from Calcino et al. (2025), Figure 6; planet panel credited to Dong et al. (2015).

sections.body: By utilizing multi-epoch scattered light observations spanning multi-year timescales, it is actually possible to measure how quickly spiral arms move. This has actually been done in observations of a disc around a young star known as MWC 758. The observations suggest the spiral arms in this system are moving much slower than we would expect if they were launched by a planet. Perhaps this is suggesting that infall is at play in this system!

Modeling infall around AB Aurigae

AB Aurigae is a young star surrounded by a disc with striking spiral arms. It is also receiving fresh gas. In an observational study led by Jessica Speedie, which I coauthored, we traced three streams towards the disc and identified a region where two of them appear to merge with it.

Telescopes can measure gas motion as well as its location. Small shifts in the wavelength of light reveal whether gas is moving towards or away from us. Maps of that motion around AB Aur show bends and wiggles, rather than the smooth pattern expected from gas travelling in circular orbits.

These disturbances had been interpreted as evidence for gravitational instability: a disc so massive that its own gravity helps gather gas into spiral arms. In our follow-up paper on AB Aur, we asked whether infall could produce similar signals. Our simulations recreated key features of the disturbed gas motion without including the gravity of the gas itself.

This means that those signals alone cannot establish whether a disc is gravitationally unstable. Infall offers another explanation. The two processes could also happen together, so our result does not rule out gravitational instability.

Connecting the spirals and the dust ring

We also explored a model combining infall with a second star orbiting inside the disc's central gap. Together, they reproduced many features of AB Aur's spiral pattern and dust ring. The comparison below shows what this model would look like through a telescope. It is a promising explanation, rather than an exact match, and the proposed companion star has not been detected.

sections.alt: Observations of AB Aurigae on the left and simulated telescope images on the right, both showing spiral structure and a ring of dust.
sections.caption: Observations on the left; our model on the right. The coloured images show starlight scattered by dust, while the overlaid contours trace the dust's millimetre emission. Calcino, Price & Ormel (2026), Figure 6. Observational data: Boccaletti et al. (2020) and Speedie et al. (2024, 2025).

sections.body: Understanding how discs respond to their surroundings helps us interpret the structures we see in them. Before attributing a spiral to an unseen planet or to the disc's own gravity, we need to consider the gas arriving from outside.

subtitle: From theory to application: Modeling infall around AB Aurigae
summary: The discs where planets form can keep receiving gas from their surroundings. What happens when that fresh material arrives? In Anatomy of a Fall and my follow-up work on AB Aurigae, I explore how incoming streams create spiral arms and disturb the motion of gas—and how to recognise these effects in telescope observations.

thumbnail.caption: AB Aurigae observed (left) and simulated (right). Calcino, Price & Ormel (2026).

description: How streams of fresh gas reshape planet-forming discs, from Anatomy of a Fall to the spirals around AB Aurigae.
